Assessment incorporating SLOOS:
- The FOMC’s March 2019 statement is balanced but dovish-leaning: growth has slowed, inflation is muted (energy-driven drag; core near 2%), and the Committee will be patient while keeping the funds rate at 2.25–2.50%.
- January 2019 SLOOS points to a more restrictive credit impulse: banks tightened standards for C&I loans and construction/land development loans; reported wider loan rate spreads; and saw weaker demand across business loans, residential real estate, HELOCs, and construction lending. Standards for key household categories (GSE-eligible mortgages, HELOCs, autos) were largely unchanged, but banks reported tighter standards for some consumer loans and expect deterioration in performance for mortgages and nonprime consumer credit. Banks also expect tighter standards for C&I and CRE and weaker business loan demand over 2019.
- These SLOOS signals reinforce the FOMC’s patience by indicating tighter credit supply and softer loan demand, consistent with slower capex and household spending. This nudges the overall assessment slightly more dovish than the baseline macro read.
